translations.text: Teaching of our blessed father Basil of Caesarea, which he delivered in a time of famine and drought.
"The lion roars, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?"
Let us make a prophetic saying the beginning of our discourse, and let us bring in the God-clad Amos as a helper for this present matter,
we who wish to give good counsel, for he healed sufferings resembling these sufferings that have come upon us.
For this prophet, in those times when that people abandoned the worship of God, trampled on the holiness of the law, and turned aside to the service of idols,
then became a preacher of repentance, taught them to turn back, and threatened them with the punishment for ungodliness.
But I pray that, for however long we have been emulating the deeds of the people of the old Scripture, an end such as theirs may not come upon us.
For that people became disobedient and, like an unbroken colt, bit on the bridle and would not come toward what was better,
but turned aside from the straight way and ran so disorderly and despised its guide, until it fell among cliffs and precipices and, as its disobedience deserved, received complete destruction.
May this not happen to you, O my children, you who were begotten through the Gospel, you whom I swaddled with the blessing of my hands.
Rather, may there be among you an obedient ear and a faithful soul, one that receives teaching well and yields to the speaker, as wax yields to the one who seals it,

so that in this way I too may receive the gladdening fruit of my labors, and you, at the time of your departure from here, may find your reward, and may then praise my teachings and be grateful to me who taught you.
What then is the cause of our discourse, for the sake of which we are speaking and which we do not yet reveal, while your souls are still waiting and are held up in that hope of hearing?
We see the sky, brothers, outspread, naked and cloudless, which makes distressing this clearness
that we longed for before, when for a long time it was covered with cloud and the sun was invisible to us.
And the earth is parched beyond measure, ugly to look at, barren of fruits and empty, with its splitting; it is cracked open and takes the brightness of the sun into its depths.
And the springs, those rich and unfailing ones, have failed us, and the wealth of the great rivers has been exhausted.
And small children cross them on foot, and women go over with their loads, and for many even drinking water has run short, and our life is one of hardship.
We have become new Israelites, seekers of a new Moses and of a wonder-working rod,
that he may again strike the rocks and comfort this thirsty people, and that wondrous clouds may come and give manna, that strange food, to men.
Now therefore let us be afraid, lest we become a tale of famine before those who have fruitful harvests.
I saw the fields and shed many tears over their barrenness, for since no rain came upon us,
some of the seeds had withered before sprouting and had remained just so,
as the farmer had left them, and others had sprouted a little and at once had pitifully wilted from the heat.
And now, who has spoken that saying of the Gospel in altered form: "The laborers are many, but the harvest is not even small"?
But the laborers, sitting on the plowed fields, have clasped their hands around their knees, which is the posture of mourners, and they weep over their vain labors.
They look at their little children and lament, they look at their wives and mourn, they take in their hands the green shoots of wheat
that have turned into dry hay, and they sigh bitterly, like fathers whose sons have died.
Let it be said then to us as well, by that same prophet whom we mentioned a little earlier, who says:
"I withheld the rain from you three months before the harvest; and I will rain, and one portion will be watered, and the portion on which I do not rain will dry up.
Two or three cities gathered together to drink water and were not satisfied, for you did not turn back to me, says the Lord."
Now then, let us learn that because of our turning away and our negligence God has sent all this upon us,
not in order to lay us waste, but in order to turn us back, as good fathers do with negligent sons,
who become angry with their sons and punish them, not in order to do them harm, but in order to turn them back from childish folly.
Do you see, then, how the multitude of our sins has changed even the seasons from their proper natures and made their temperate mixtures foreign to what is natural?
For the winter did not have moisture along with dryness, as is usual, but it bound everything with frost and dried it out, and it was devoid of dew and rain.
Again, the days of spring showed that one nature of theirs, which is heat, but did not display moisture at all.
Rather, heat and cold went beyond their measure, and to our harm they have borne witness to one another [?], and they bring people to destruction.
What then is the cause of this disorder? What is this innovation in the nature of the seasons?
Let us inquire as people of understanding, and let us consider as rational beings. Can it be that there is no ruler of all things?
Can it be that God, the skillful maker of all things, has forgotten his providence for us? Can it be that authority and power have been taken away from him?
Or does he have the same power and is not deprived of authority, yet has he come in harshness and changed that great goodness and mercy which he had toward us into hatred of humankind?
May none of these things be so! No person who is master of his reason could say any of these things.
But the causes on account of which we are not in our usual state are known and clear: namely, that what we receive from him we do not give to others.
We praise charity and ourselves never practice it; we are set free from slavery and we show no mercy to our fellow slaves;
when hungry we are fed, and we pass by the hungry; we who have God as a treasury generously given have become greedy and evil toward the poor;
our sheep bear in abundance, and the naked are more numerous than the sheep;
the storehouses are cramped by the abundance of what lies in them, and we show no mercy to the one who is in straits.
For this reason he brings upon us this just judgment; for this reason God too does not open his hand to us, because we have driven out brotherly love.
For this reason our water-jars are dry: because love has dried up.
The voice of those making litany cries out in vain and is scattered into the air, because neither did we listen to the entreaty of those who entreated us.
Fathers, all of you, apart from a few, are given over to trade; mothers, you serve in the service of mammon.
Few are with me in prayer, and even these, faint-hearted and yawning, turn this way and that and are eager
for the moment when the psalmist will finish the verses, or when they may escape from the church as from a prison and leave behind the hardship of prayer.
As for these little children, who have left their schoolbooks behind, they regard this occasion as joy and rest, and this sorrow of ours seems to them a festival,
because for a short time they have been set free from the harshness of the teacher and the difficulty of their lessons.
But the multitude of grown men, that assembly guilty of sins, goes about the city loose and unrestrained,
those who have in their souls the cause of the evils, who stirred up and brought about this trial.
And the unknowing and innocent infants come to the confession of God, who can understand neither the cause of these hardships nor how to pray as one should.
You, come here with me, you who are defiled by sin; you, fall down before God, and weep and sigh; leave the infant alone, and let him do what is proper for his age.
Why do you, the accused, hide yourself and send the guiltless one to give an account?
Is the Judge to be scorned, that you should send someone else and that he should take that person for you?
It was right for the child to come as well, but with you and not alone. Do you not see
how the Ninevites, when they repented of their sins and entreated God, when Jonah preached to them after the sea and the whale,
did not merely bring the infants to repentance while they themselves stayed in pleasure and ease? Rather, fasting first humbled the fathers,
who had sinned and who were being punished; and for the sake of greater repentance the infants too were made to weep by force,
so that this sorrow and mourning might reach every age, those with understanding and those without it, some willingly and some unwillingly.
And so God saw them humbled, who had brought wretchedness and hardship upon every kind,
and he had mercy on them and refrained from destroying them, and he granted joy to those who mourned with understanding.
Oh, that swift repentance! Oh, that wise and steadfast distress!
They did not even leave the animals unafflicted, but contrived that they too should cry out, when they separated the calf from its mother and the lamb from the sheep,
and the nursing child was no longer in its mother's bosom, but the young were on one side and the mothers on the other, and from all of them came pitiful cries, outdoing one another.
The hungry young sought those springs of milk; the mothers in turn were cut to the heart by their natural love and called to their offspring with pitiful voices.
Again the infants, pressed by hunger, would cry out with weeping, and the hearts of the parents would melt with natural compassion.
For this reason also the divine word recorded their repentance as a pattern for life: for among them the old men lamented and tore at their gray hairs,
the young men repented more vigorously, the poor sighed, and the rich forgot their wealth and luxury and they too took up struggle and weeping;
their king exchanged his glory for dishonor, cast aside his crown and put ashes on his head, stripped off the purple and put on sackcloth,
left his lofty throne and sat on the ground, put royal glory far from him and lamented with the people,
and became like one among the others, when he saw the wrath of the King of all.
This is the mind of wise servants. Such is the repentance of those who have sinned.
But we sin mightily, and when it comes to repentance we are fainthearted and slack.
Who pours out tears in prayer, so that in this way rain and good dew may come?
Who blots out his sins and, like blessed David, drenches his bed with tears?
Who has moistened the feet of strangers and washed off the dust of the road, so that in a time of drought, when he entreats God, God may hear him and give rain?
Who has brought up one of the children of our father, so that God may now make our wheat flourish, which, like an orphan, is oppressed by the winds?
Who has stretched out a hand to the afflicted widow in the afflictions of this life, so that what she needs may be duly given to her?
Tear up the unjust bond, so that in this way sin may be loosed; blot out the record of those heavy interest charges, so that the earth may bring forth its natural vegetation.
For when bronze and silver and gold, which by nature are barren, depart from their own nature and begin to give birth,
then that which by nature is rich in offspring becomes barren and, for the punishment of those who live on it, takes on unfruitfulness.
Now therefore let those who honor greed show what the power of the wealth they have hoarded is,
or what use it will be to them, if God is angered and makes this punishment still more severe.
Those who gather gold will become yellower than gold, if they do not have the bread that yesterday and the day before was contemptible in their eyes because of the abundance.
But say this: if there is no seller, and no wheat in your storehouses, what use will those heavy pieces of gold be?
Is it not buried with them? Is gold not earth and useless clay, and will it not perish with that clay, your body?
You have acquired everything, and the one thing better than all you do not have: the power to feed yourself.
With all that wealth of yours make one cloud; procure a flow of a little dew;
by some means change the earth back to fruitfulness; by that arrogant and vain wealth undo this trial.
Perhaps you will entreat one of the servants of God, so that by his prayer, like Elijah the Tishbite, he may give you relief from these evils:
a destitute man, dried up, without shoes, without a home, without possessions, clothed in a single garment, as Elijah was in his mantle, who has prayer as his constant companion,
Fasting as your table-companion: if you should meet with the help of such a one, would you not hold that great wealth of yours in contempt? Would you not spit upon gold?
Would you not cast away silver like dung, silver which before all else you used to call powerful and beloved, and which in the time of need you found to be a powerless helper?

This trial has come about because of you: because you had and did not give, because you passed by the hungry, because you did not turn toward the one who wept, because you had no mercy on the one who bowed down before you.
Evil comes upon a people even on account of a few, as when Achan stole and that whole multitude was punished.
Zimri fornicated with the Midianites, and Israel was condemned.
Therefore let all of us, both individually and in common, examine ourselves; let us look to this famine as to a teacher. Let each of us call to mind his own sins.
Let us too say with understanding that word of blessed Job: "The hand of the Lord has touched me," and let us ascribe the trial to our sins.
But if another cause must also be stated, let us say that often such grievous sufferings come upon people also to test their souls,
so that in this way those who are tested may be revealed, whether rich or poor, for both are well tested by patience,
and especially at this time: the one, if he is merciful and loves his brethren, and the other, if he is thankful and no blasphemer, and does not change his mind along with the affairs of this life.
For I have seen with my own eyes many people who, as long as the affairs of this world went prosperously for them,
give some small thanks to the Benefactor, even if not in full measure;
but if affairs turn otherwise even a little, and the rich man becomes poor, and the one strong in body becomes sick, and the glorious and honored becomes disgraced and despised,
then they change and become ungrateful, they speak blasphemous words, they grow negligent toward prayer, as though toward a debtor who delays payment,
and so they accuse God, and do not fall down before him as before an angered king. But let no such thought be in your mind!
Rather, when you see that God does not give you the good things of this world, consider thus within yourself, according to custom, and say:
"Can it be that God is unable to give me food, or anything else? And how could that be?
He who is Lord of heaven and earth and of all things, the wise ordainer of the seasons of the years, the governor of all things, by whom,
as in a well-ordered array, the changes of the seasons have been so arranged that by their variety they may provide for our need in various ways.
And now there is moisture in its proper season, and then heat comes after it, and cold is mingled with warmth, and dryness comes again in its own season.
God, then, is powerful, since he is confessed to be powerful. Can it be, then, that goodness is lacking in him?
Nor can this statement be made either, for what necessity persuaded one who was not good to create man in the beginning?
Or who compelled the Creator, against his will, to take earth and make such beauty out of clay?
Who forced him to give reason to man as his own image, so that in this way he might receive instruction in skill and learn heavenly wisdom and the expression of things he has not seen?"
And when you reflect in this way, you will find goodness, which is with God and has not failed until now, nor will it ever fail.
If not, tell me, what was there to prevent this from being not a drought but a complete burning?
Might not the sun have altered its accustomed course only slightly, drawn only slightly nearer the earth, and burned up everything visible in a single moment?
Or might he not have rained fire from heaven, as upon those other sinners to whom he did this? Come to yourself and to your senses, O man!
Do not act like foolish children, who, when their teacher becomes angry with them, tear up their books;
or who, when their father keeps them from food for their own benefit, tear their clothes or scratch their mother's face with their nails.
Do you not know that winter tests the ship's captain, battle the soldier, the battle line the general, and trial the Christian, and that sorrow tests the soul, as fire tests gold?
If you are poor, do not become sorrowful and despairing, for immoderate grief becomes a cause of sin,
for sorrow drowns the mind and turns it toward despair, and despair begets ingratitude.
Rather, have hope in God. Does he not see that distress of yours?
He has food in his hands and delays giving it, so that your steadfastness may be tested and your mind may be revealed, whether it is like that of the ungrateful, who,
as long as food is in their mouths, give thanks and marvel and glorify, but if the table is lacking for even a short time, they pelt with words of blasphemy as if with stones.
Read through the old law and the new, and you will find many who were marvelously nourished by God:

Elijah was on Carmel, that high and impassable mountain, a desert-dweller in the desert, and the soul alone of that righteous man was altogether rich, and as provision for his life he had hope in God.
And while he was living in this way, he did not die of hunger; rather, those birds, more gluttonous and rapacious than all other birds,
brought him food and served that righteous man. Those that by habit snatch the food of others
changed their nature at the command of the King and became faithful keepers of that bread and meat, for we have learned from Scripture that they brought it to him.
Again, that pit of Babylon held the Israelite youth, a captive through trial but noble in soul and mind.
And lions were with him, and they fasted contrary to their nature.
And Habakkuk traveled through the air, for an angel carried that man along with the food, and so that the righteous man might not be distressed by hunger,
he crossed in a short time all the many lands and seas that lie between Judea and Babylon.
Again, what will you say of the people in the desert, whose leader was Moses? How did they live during those forty years?
There was no man there sowing, nor ox drawing the plow, nor threshing floor, nor winepress.
And they had food unsown and unreaped, and the rock brought forth springs, which had not existed before but sprang up then.
I forgo telling of each of those whom God, like a father, nourished in hardship; but you, be patient for a little while in that trial of yours, like valiant Job.
And do not be swept away by the waves; do not throw away anything of the cargo of the virtues.
Keep thanksgiving in your soul like a cargo of great price, and through thanksgiving you will receive twofold good.
Remember the word of the Apostle, who says: "In everything give thanks."
If you are poor, there is another poorer than you; if you have food for ten days, he has it for one.
As a good man, make up his lack from your surplus and so make things even.
Do not be negligent about giving from the little you have; do not honor your own comfort above that of another.
Even if your food comes down to a single loaf and a beggar comes to your door,
take that one loaf out of your store, place it on your hands, lift your eyes to heaven, and speak a good word of supplication, saying:
"Behold, this is one loaf, Lord, as you see, and this trial is plain, but I honor your commandment more than myself, and from this little I give to this hungry brother;
you too, give mercy to this afflicted servant of yours. I know your goodness, I trust also in your power; you do not put off your grace, but you give the gift whenever you wish."
If you speak and act in this way, the bread that you give out of your distress will become seed for the harvest.
It will bring forth manifold fruit; it will become a pledge of good and a procurer of mercy.
You too, say the word of the widow of Sidon; in similar circumstances, remember that event at the proper time:
"As the Lord lives, I have only this in my house as food for myself and my children."
If you give from it, you too will have that horn of oil flowing by grace and that jar of flour that is never emptied.
For the grace of God toward believers is like springs that pour forth continually and do not run dry, and it gives back everything twofold.
Lend, you poor man, to the rich God; believe him who always counts what is given to the poor and afflicted as given to himself, and who pays the reward.
He is a trustworthy guarantor, whose treasures are spread out over sea and dry land.
And you will receive what is owed from him even in the heart of the sea. If you ask for it, he will give you the principal with the interest and will heal that sickness of hunger.
For hunger is a pitiable suffering; hunger is the chief of trials. For the other evils take one out of life quickly:
the sword brings the end quickly, the force of fire swiftly extinguishes life, and beasts, if they come upon someone, quickly crush him with their teeth,
but the evil of hunger is slow, its wound long-lasting, and its sickness stubborn and hard; it has death always at hand and does not snatch one away quickly,
but it dries up the natural moisture, cools the heat, thins the bulk of the body, and withers the strength.
The flesh becomes like a spider's web; the color on the bones has no bloom, for the redness flees as the blood drains away;
there is no whiteness, for the affliction blackens it; instead the flesh becomes livid, pitiably mixed with yellow and black;
From that suffering the knees cannot bear the body, but bend this way and that, about to fall; the voice is thin and weak;
the eyes are feeble and sunken, lying uselessly in their sockets; the bones are drier than greens and the tips of trees;
the belly is empty and wasted, having no natural thickness of the waist, but is pitifully nailed to the bones of the back.
Now then, whoever passes by such a body, how many evils does he deserve? Or what is the measure of his mercilessness?
Or how does he not deserve to be counted among savage beasts, and to perish as one defiled and a murderer?
For whoever has the power to heal some evil and willingly does not provide its healing, out of greed, will justly be condemned as the very perpetrator of that evil.
The suffering of hunger has many times compelled many to transgress the boundaries of nature and to lay hands on human flesh, those who share their own nature:
and a mother takes back into her belly, pitifully and wickedly, the one she bore from her own womb.
And this deed was revealed by the ordeal of the Jews, which the diligent Josephus has written down for us,
when those evil sufferings came upon the people of Jerusalem as judgment for the lawlessness they committed against the Lord. Do you see our God himself?
For he many times passed by those other afflictions, but he had great pity on the hungry and said: "I have pity on this people."
For this reason too, at the last judgment, when the Lord calls the righteous, he first calls the merciful one, the one who feeds the hungry, the giver of bread;
and so the good man receives life before others, and the merciless and greedy man is handed over to torment before all other sinners.
Behold, this time calls you to that mother of the commandments, and take great care that the time of trading and exchange does not pass by,
for time runs and does not wait for the one who comes late; the days go by and pass the negligent man.
And just as there is no turning a river back upstream, unless you get there first and take what you need of its water,
so too time cannot be turned back or held fast, unless you get ahead of it and take profit from it.
For this reason I tell you to catch up with that commandment, as with something fleeing, and to carry it out.
And take hold of it from every side and gather it into your bosom; give a little and gain much.
Undo that first sin by mercy and by giving food, for as Adam ate wickedly and committed sin,
so let us wipe out that sin of eating, if we feed a hungry brother.
O peoples, listen, Christians, give ear: all this is said by the Lord, who is the speaker and who uses the lips of his servants as instruments.
Let us who are endowed with reason not become more savage than these brute animals. For they by nature use in common what springs up from the earth:
flocks of many sheep graze on one mountain, and many horses move about on one plain, and none of them prevents another from taking its food,
but we take for ourselves what is common, what belongs to many, and we alone consume it.
Let us be put to shame by the deeds of the pagans, among whom love of humanity is practiced.
Among some of them there is a law of mercy, and they have one table, and their whole multitude shares all things in common.
Let us leave aside those outside and look at those three thousand and their deeds.
Let us become like that first assembly of Christians, among whom all things were held in common:
life and souls, unity, a common table, undivided brotherhood, love without duplicity, which made their many bodies one and joined their separate souls together.
You have many examples of brotherly love from the old and new Scriptures.
If you see an old man hungry, call him and feed him, as Joseph did for Jacob.
If you find your enemy in want [?], do not take revenge on him in enmity, but feed him, as he did for those brothers by whom he had been sold.
If you see a young man in distress, weep over him, as he wept over Benjamin, the son of old age.
Perhaps greed will tempt you and press you hard, as the queen did Joseph.
It drags at your garment, so that you may disregard the commandment and come to love that which loves the world and loves gold more than the commandment of the King.
But when a thought comes upon you that fights against the commandment and defiles that holy mind with love of silver, and it compels you to abandon brotherly love,
you too leave your garment with it and go away in anger; keep faith toward the Lord, as he did toward Potiphar.
Provide for that want for one year, as he did for those seven years. Do not grant everything to desire; give something to the soul as well.
And count two daughters as your own: this pleasure of the world and eternal life.
If you will not give everything to the better one, then at least divide it in half between the harlot child and the pure one.
Do not show the life of this world overflowing with wealth and the life of the age to come naked and clothed in old rags.
When you must be presented before Christ and come before the face of the Judge in the guise of a bride, and your name is to be that life of virtue,
beware lest you present the bride, your soul, before the Bridegroom ugly and unadorned, so that when he sees her ugliness he turns his face away, loathes her, and rejects union with her.
Rather, adorn her with fitting adornment and keep her beautiful in expectation of that great wedding,
so that she too may light her lamp with those wise virgins, when she has the unquenchable fire of understanding and does not lack the oil of the virtues;
so that the God-inspired prophecy may be confirmed in deed, and that saying may be fulfilled upon your soul, which declares:
"The queen stood at your right hand, adorned in gold-woven raiment and clothed in many colors, beautiful.
Listen, daughter, and see, incline your ear, and may the King delight in your beauty."
For the prophet said this about nature, and he was proclaiming the goodness of the nature of the soul, its beauty.
But it is fulfilled upon the soul of each person, for the assembly of the church is made up of each individual.
Consider well this passing world and that eternal one. Do not give up those eternal good things and take evil wealth for yourself.
For it will leave you, in your flesh, and go away, and it will remain in this world as a memorial of mercilessness.
But at the coming of the terrible Judge, who is undoubtedly to come, you will then have stripped yourself of honor and eternal glory and opened
to it the unquenchable fire and Gehenna and the other torments, bitter and eternal in their pains, in place of that endless and blessed life.
But do not think that I am frightening you with a lie, as mothers and nurses do with little children: when they see them crying, they quiet them with lying words.
These words are not a fable but true, proclaimed beforehand by the One who does not lie.
And attend well to that word of the Gospel which says: Of these words not one iota or one hair shall pass away.
Rather, the body too, wasted away in the grave, will rise, and the soul, separated from it by death,
will dwell again in that body, and the true exposure of deeds will be presented, when no others will bear witness, but the inner mind itself.
And to each will be given according to his desert by the righteous Judge, for to him belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
